summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) by integrating Hi-C data with RNA-seq from 18 patients and 4 healthy controls. judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) by integrating Hi-C data with RNA-seq from 18 patients and 4 healthy controls. The researchers found that 3D genome organization at compartment, topologically associated domain (TAD), and loop levels could hierarchically classify T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectories. Approximately 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL were associated with these structural alterations. The study identified 34 novel translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new loops, revealing a mechanism of translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking that activates the HOXA cluster. Specifically, ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13 genes, rather than other HOXA genes, was linked to immature phenotypes and poor clinical outcomes. The findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring is a critical driver of T-ALL etiology and prognosis, potentially offering new therapeutic targets like anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors for high-risk subgroups.

Research Context
3D genome alterations are known to drive tumorigenesis. However, their specific role in T-ALL remains unclear. T-ALL is characterized by diverse transcription factor dysregulation. Prior studies focused on coding mutations, ignoring noncoding drivers. Understanding 3D structure could reveal new subtypes.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can 3D genome alterations classify T-ALL subtypes? Do structural changes drive gene expression in T-ALL? Are there novel translocations affecting noncoding regions? Does enhancer hijacking explain HOXA cluster activation? Do specific HOXA genes predict poor prognosis?

Methodological Details
Study included 18 T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls. Leukemia blasts were purified via FACS analysis. RNA-seq used TruSeq kits with 15 million read pairs. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample. Data was aligned to hg19 using TopHat and HTSeq. Differential expression required FDR <0.01 and fold change >2. Compartment analysis used eigenvector command at 100 kb. TAD boundaries were calculated using Insulation score method. Loops were detected using HiCCUPS with FDR <0.1. Translocations were identified using hic_breakfinder.

Procedures And Architectures
RNA-seq libraries were prepared with TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2. Hi-C raw data were processed by the in-house HiCpipe framework. ChIA-PET2 was used to trim bridge linkers. Juicer was applied to generate contact matrices. Knight-Ruiz normalization was used for compartment/TAD analysis. Differential TAD boundaries used t-test FDR<0.01. Loop anchors were analyzed by GREAT for enrichment. Translocation breakpoints were refined to single base-pair resolution. Novel translocations required breakpoints not near known ones. Visualization was generated using pyGenomeTracks and Juicebox.

Key Results
3D genome organization classified T-ALL subtypes hierarchically. 45% of upregulated genes were associated with 3D alterations. 29% of DEGs were linked to structural changes. ETP and non-ETP ALLs were separated at the loop level. Pearson correlation of 0.685 linked loop changes to expression. 34 novel translocations were identified in noncoding regions. 44 new loops formed between translocated chromosomes. HOXA11-A13 expression linked to poor survival. HOXA13+ status predicted overall survival independently. HOXA11-A13+ cases showed DN and ETP phenotypes.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
3D alterations rewired the T-ALL transcriptome. Translocations mediate enhancer hijacking of transcription factors. HOXA cluster activation drives immature phenotypes. Specific HOXA genes define high-risk clinical entities. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit HOXA11-A13+ patients.

Contradictions And Limitations
Sample size was limited to 18 patients. Some samples fell between ETP and non-ETP categories. Translocation detection relied on Hi-C depth limitations. Ethical approval details were not fully specified in text. Code availability was not explicitly stated.

Claims
3D genome alterations drive T-ALL development via enhancer hijacking. Translocations form new loops between chromosomes. Hijacked enhancers activate T-ALL transcription factors. HOXA11-A13 expression correlates with poor prognosis. Not all HOXA genes drive poor outcomes. TLX positivity had no association with outcome. New therapeutic targets for high-risk T-ALL. Need for subtype-specific treatments.
HOXA11-A13 expression defines a distinct high-risk T-ALL subgroup. HOXA11-A13+ cases showed DN and ETP phenotypes. HOXA13+ status predicted overall survival independently. These cases had higher JAK-STAT pathway mutations. HOXA9 was not associated with poor outcomes. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this group.

Data And Code Availability
Hi-C data could be deposited as contact matrices. MATLAB code was used for heatmaps and plots. Raw RNA-seq data for cell lines downloaded from GEO.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Differential loops called with FDR <0.1. TAD boundaries defined by detection in at least two conditions. Translocations manually assessed after filtering controls.

Ethical Considerations
Samples collected under protocol approved by ethics committee. Peripheral blood obtained under ethics committee approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a showed PCA of 3D genome and transcriptome. Figure 3a displayed translocations in Hi-C maps. Figure 5 illustrated enhancer hijacking mechanisms. Figure 6 showed survival analysis for HOXA subtypes.

Three Takeaways
3D genome alterations classify T-ALL subtypes and drive oncogenesis. HOXA11-A13 ectopic expression defines a high-risk, incurable subgroup. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking is a key mechanism.
